title_content.content: Energy Oriented Three-Tier Computation Offloading Scheme in Maritime Edge Computing Network

paragraph_content.content: Hongxia Zhang , Shiyu Xi , Bodong Shang , Member, IEEE, Peiying Zhang , Member, IEEE, Sheng Wu , Member, IEEE, and Chunxiao Jiang , Fellow, IEEE

Abstract—With the development of maritime continuing to grow, large-scale maritime wireless devices (MWDs) are being deployed for various maritime applications. The rapid development of maritime Internet of Things (IoT) and growing demand for these applications have led to an increasing number of computation-intensive and resource-sensitive tasks. Considering the limited computing capacity and energy of MWDs, it is challenging to transmit and process massive maritime computing tasks in an energy efficient manner. In this paper, we propose a three-tier maritime edge computing system in which low earth orbit (LEO) satellite and offshore base station (OBS) support to provide communication and computing services for MWDs. The system optimizes association variable, task partitioning, transmission power, and computing resource allocation to reduce system energy consumption under latency constraints. The optimization problem is formulated as a mixed integer non-linear programming (MINLP) optimization problem. We decompose the original problem into four subproblems and design algorithms to solve them. Firstly, the association variable optimization subproblem is solved by slack variable method. Then, we adopt quadratic transformation and design a difference of convex algorithm to solve transmission power optimization subproblem. Further, task partitioning subproblem is solved by obtaining upper and lower bounds of offloading task size by strict deduction, and then solved by the standard convex method. Finally, Lagrangian dual method is utilized to deal with joint computing resource optimization subproblem of LEO satellite and OBS. In simulation results, the proposed algorithm saves 39.3% of system energy consumption compared to benchmark schemes.
Index Terms—Maritime network, edge computing, LEO satellite network, computation offloading.

W ITH the gradual popularization of 5 G mobile com-munications, it has facilitated the continuous and pros- munications,it has facilitated the continuous and prosperous development of maritime applications such as maritime transportation, maritime exploration, and environmental monitoring [1]. Meanwhile, the development of maritime Internet of Things (IoT) has driven the massive deployment of maritime wireless devices (MWDs) and the rapid growth in demand for mobile applications. The emergence of large-scale resourceintensive and latency-sensitive tasks has posed great challenges to the limited computing capacity of MWDs. Furthermore, MWDs have limited battery capacity, which significantly reduces battery life for long-term execution of overloaded and energy-intensive computing tasks [2]. Therefore, it is significant how to utilize the limited network resources in maritime communication systems to improve computing performance.

Maritime communication systems and terrestrial communication systems have obvious differences in terms of network architecture and network resources. In terrestrial communication systems, network infrastructures, such as base stations and cloud computing centers, have been widely deployed, providing beneficial conditions for ready access to IoT devices. Maritime communication is usually based on shore-based communication facilities, such as maritime weather stations, which are located on offshore islands or isolated islands. However, space and geographical factors restrict the deployment of shore-based communication facilities, which makes it difficult to install and deploy computationally capable servers. On the other hand, shore-based communications have limited coverage areas and suffer from disadvantages such as high communication costs and low bandwidth. Moreover, long-distance transmission results in long latency and high energy consumption, which cannot meet the rapidly growing demand for communication and computation [3]. In recent years, the rapid development of low earth orbit (LEO) satellites has provided a new solution to the above challenges.

The development of space communication networks has brought unprecedented attention to LEO satellites. LEO satellite communication has made great strides in commercial, civil, and military applications. SpaceX, Amazon, and other companies are making great efforts to build LEO satellite constellations to achieve seamless global coverage. Benefiting from the multiaccess edge computing (MEC), satellite edge computing (SEC) serves as an emerging computing paradigm [4]. Therefore, maritime IoT devices can offload tasks to LEO satellite for processing, alleviating the computational and energy burden.

Partial offloading is recognized in MEC as a computational paradigm. The communication and computing resources of the LEO satellites are still limited, making it impractical to offload all tasks to the LEO satellites for processing. On the other hand, MWDs offload massive task size, generates additional transmission energy and latency. LEO satellites and OBS can utilize solar energy as an energy supply, but communication and daily operation consume a large amount of energy. Therefore, it is crucial to reduce unnecessary energy waste through energy consumption optimization to improve the life cycle and operational efficiency of LEO satellites and OBS. Thus, partial offloading is more meaningful in reducing system energy consumption while satisfying latency constraints.

MEC technology provides a promising solution for computation offloading. Qin et al. [5] investigated the perceptual computation offloading scheme, which considered the stochastic nature of the UAV task generation sequence and server load to optimize offloading strategy and resource assignment. Chen et al. [6] researched task offloading in distributed networks, where device associations, offloading decisions, and trajectories are optimized to maximize the quality of experience. Liu et al. [7] proposed a multivariate nonlinear coupled latency minimization problem to reduce latency by optimizing cache resource assignment. Gao et al. [8] optimized offloading strategy for devices using attention-weighted graph recurrent networks, which improved the generalization ability of offloading scheme. Pham et al. [9] studied a vehicle assisted computing system, where devices offload partial task to servers or nearby vehicles for maximizing offloading utility of mobile devices. Shen et al. [10] investigated a UAV-assisted computing system, where UAVs can process tasks for IoT devices to minimize energy consumption. Jiang et al. [11] explored network slicing, resource allocation, and introducing a two-level slicing model to maximize successful processing rate.

The research on satellite edge computing has yielded many significant achievements. Lakew et al. [12] studied a LEOenabled network model where multiple LEO satellites provide computing services to resource-constrained energy harvesting UAVs. Nguyen et al. [13] investigated a hybrid computing system, which optimizes offloading decision and resource optimization to reduce weighted computing energy consumption. Wang et al. [14] proposed a computation offloading scheme by optimizing offloading selection and resource allocation to minimize weighted energy consumption. Cheng et al. [15] proposed a satellite dynamic offloading strategy to minimize the overall mission completion time by optimizing task offloading and resource allocation. Gao et al. [16] studied the multi-user computation offloading problem, which minimizes the system overhead by optimizing offloading strategy and transmission power. Ding et al. [17] proposed the satellite-terrestrial assisted multi-tier computing network to reduce computing energy consumption. Zhang et al. [18] proposed a distributed offloading scheme that employs a counterfactual multi-agent policy gradient scheme to minimize latency. Zhang et al. [19] studied task scheduling problem in SAGIN, in which IoT devices offload computing tasks to UAVs. The offloading strategy is optimized to minimize the energy consumption of UAVs. Zhou et al. [20] designed a distributed algorithm for efficiently solving the computation offloading problem in satellite networks. Tang et al. [21] investigated a LEO satellite-supported edge system, in which user association and computing resource are jointly optimized to reduce energy consumption.

To efficiently perform computing tasks for MWDs, many studies have explored computation offloading schemes in maritime communication networks. Dai et al. [22] presented a offshore and airborne computing scheme, which minimizes latency by optimizing offloading decisions and computing resource allocation. Dai et al. [23] proposed a maritime offloading scheme, where UAVs and surface sink nodes provide computing services for MWD. Li et al. [24] studied a maritime computation offloading by optimizing position and transmission power of unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) to reduce energy consumption. Dai et al. [25] investigated a UAV-assisted computation offloading by optimizing offloading strategy to achieve minimum energy consumption. Dai et al. [26] proposed a UAV-assisted offloading scheme with the goal of increasing the system benefits of maritime edge computing networks. Xu et al. [27] proposed a UAVbased marine offloading scheme to minimize overall latency by optimizing user scheduling and UAV trajectories, and resource allocation. Zeng et al. [28] proposed a USV computation offloading scheme and a joint task and resource allocation scheme to minimize energy consumption of USVs. Lyu et al. [29] studied a marine task offloading problem by introducing a coalitional game method to achieve a Nash equilibrium in order to minimize the system overhead.

In summary, energy consumption is typically a critical criterion for performance evaluation in SEC. However, the importance of LEO satellites for maritime communication and computation has been neglected in the past studies on computation offloading for maritime networks. Therefore, we consider the characteristics of LEO satellite and OBS and design a maritime computation scheme based on OBS and LEO satellite to provide services for MWDs. We introduce LEO satellite and an OBS into maritime edge computing network, which jointly provide communication and computing services for MWDs. Considering the strict latency constraints of tasks, we present a LEO satellite and OBS-assisted partial offloading scheme. MWDs split computing task into three parts, which are processed in local, LEO satellite, and OBS, respectively. Eventually, we optimize association variable, task partitioning, transmission power, and computing resource allocation to minimize system energy consumption. item_content.content: - Maritime edge computing system design: We design a maritime edge computing system with a three-tier computing architecture, in which LEO satellites and OBS can provide computing services for MWDs. For satisfying task latency requirements and reducing energy consumption, we adopt a partial offloading scheme to process computing tasks in parallel. MWDs can offload partial task to be processed at the LEO, and can also offload a portion of tasks to be processed at the OBS through the LEO, with the remaining tasks being processed locally.

- Problem formulation and solutions: The system energy consumption minimization problem is decomposed into four subproblems and design optimization algorithms to solve them. Specifically, we use slack variable and convex optimization methods to solve association variable. The transmission power optimization subproblem is an non-convex problem. Therefore, we transform it into a convex problem using a quadratic transformation and then solve it using a difference of convex algorithm. Then, task partitioning subproblem is solved by deriving upper and lower bounds of offloading task size based on constraints. Afterwards, the computing resource allocation subproblem is solved by using Lagrangian dual method. Finally, we design a joint iterative optimization algorithm to achieve global optimization.

paragraph_content.content: System design insights: We verify the performance and effectiveness of the proposed scheme in various environments using system energy consumption as a criterion. Simulation results show that our proposed scheme has a significant advantage in reducing the system energy consumption, with savings 39.3% of the system energy consumption compared to the benchmark schemes.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system model and defines the optimization objective. In Section III, we design an iterative algorithm to solve the system energy minimization problem. Section IV validates the performance of the proposed scheme. Finally, Section V concludes this paper.

paragraph_content.content: We consider a comparison with the following schemes to validate the performance of the proposed scheme: 1) Pure local computation (PLC): MWDs process tasks locally without offloading [36]. 2) Average LEO computing resource (ACR): LEO satellites’ computing resource are equally divided among the associated MWDs [40]. 3) Two-tier computation offloading (TTCO): LEO satellites and OBS are used to collaborate in the computation offloading, and the tasks cannot be processed locally [33]. 4) Maximum channel gain (Max-Gain): MWDs select LEO satellites with maximum channel gain, and the task can be processed locally, LEO satellite and OBS in parallel [33]. 5) Simulated annealing computation offloading scheme (SACO): Optimizing task partitioning using simulated annealing algorithm [41]. 6) Three-tier maritime computation offloading scheme (TTMCO): The proposed LEO satellite and OBS-supported computation offloading scheme in this paper.

Fig. 5 illustrates system energy consumption versus the bits of MWDs’ task. The system energy consumption of all the schemes shows an increasing trend as the task size continues to increase. Furthermore, the energy-saving advantage of TTMCO expands compared to benchmark schemes. This is because TTMCO adjusts task partitioning and computing resource allocation according to changes in task size. When tasks become too large, the computing resource of MWDs may fail to satisfy the maximum tolerable latency constraint. Consequently, when the task size exceeds 1.5 MB, PLC is unable to meet the processing requirements of tasks. To adhere to the limit of maximum tolerable latency, MWD offloads a larger portion of the task to the LEO satellite and OBS for processing, resulting in increased transmission latency. Therefore, the LEO satellites and OBS need to allocate additional computing resource to process the tasks, which leads to an increase regarding system energy consumption in the TTCO and Max-Gain schemes. On the other hand, energy consumption of TTCO gradually exceeds Max-Gain. The unreasonable task partitioning dramatically increases system energy consumption in the SACO scheme. In the ACR scheme, the computational capacity allocated to tasks by the LEO satellite is much higher than that required for processing tasks, leading to a significant increase in the system energy consumption.

chart_caption.content: Fig. 6. System energy consumption versus MWD’s number.

paragraph_content.content: Fig. 6 verifies the correlation among the number of MWDs and system energy consumption. The increase in the number of MWDs leads to an increase in the total task size of the system, which in turn leads to an upward trend in the system energy consumption of TTCO, Max-Gain, SACO, and TTMCO. TTMCO has the lowest system energy consumption compared to the benchmark scenario. This is because TTMCO considers the effect of interference and reduces energy consumption by optimizing the user association. Max-Gain adjusts the user association based on the channel gain and ignores the effect of intra-cell interference on the transmission rate, resulting in an increase in the system energy consumption. In the ACR scheme, the number of MWDs associated with LEO satellites is small at the initial stage, and the average computational capacity far exceeds the task processing requirement, resulting in high system energy consumption. As the number of MWDs increases, the average computational capacity of LEO satellites decreases. The computational capacity used for task processing is gradually reasonable, and the system energy consumption is gradually reduced. Then, the increase in the number of MWDs affects the increase in the system task size, resulting in a continued rise in system energy consumption. Compared to TTCO and SACO, the performance gap between the two schemes continues to widen. Tasks cannot be computed locally, and the increase in task size leads to an increase in the transmission latency and energy consumption of MWDs. However, the increase in transmission latency drives the need for LEO satellites or OBS to allocate more computational capacity to process tasks to satisfy latency constraints.

chart_caption.content: Fig. 7. System energy consumption versus LEO satellites’ altitude.

paragraph_content.content: Fig. 7 compares the performance of computation offloading schemes at different LEO satellite altitudes. System energy consumption of all schemes shows an increasing trend as LEO satellite orbit altitude increases. The increase in satellite altitude leads to a larger transmission distance and more energy is consumed for task offloading. Furthermore, LEO satellites need to allocate more computing resource to meet the maximum tolerable latency constraint. Compared to ACR, TTCO, Max-Gain, and SACO, TTMCO has the lowest system energy consumption. This can be attributed to TTMCO can adjust the task partitioning, user association and resource allocation according to LEO satellites’ altitude, providing a more reasonable and flexible offloading strategy to optimize the system energy consumption. In ACR scheme, the equalization strategy of computational capacity allocated by LEO satellite to associated MWDs exceeds the task processing requirements and consumes more system energy. In Max-Gain scheme, the user association is determined by channel gain, which tends to cause MWDs aggregations. The limited bandwidth of LEO satellites affects the transmission rate between MWDs and LEO satellites, thus increasing energy consumption. The increase in LEO satellite altitude affects the transmission latency for task offloading. In TTCO and SACO schemes, more tasksize are usually processed on the LEO satellites to meet the latency constraints. LEO satellites allocate more computing resource to process tasks resulting in increased energy consumption. It’s crucial to employ reasonable user association, task partitioning, and resource allocation strategies to mitigate system energy consumption.

Fig. 8 compares number of LEO satellites and system energy consumption at different computational capacities of MWDs. The computational capability of MWDs and the number of LEO satellites have an impact on system energy consumption. System energy consumption is decreasing along with the deployment scale of LEO satellites. LEO satellites have limited communication resource. The growing number of LEO satellites provides more access possibilities to MWDs, which reduces the possibility of MWDs aggregation. Additionally, there exists a positive correlation between the computational capability of MWDs and system energy consumption. This is particularly significant in scenarios where tasks cannot be entirely offloaded to LEO satellites or OBS for processing due to the necessity of meeting maximum tolerable latency requirements. Moreover, the augmentation of local computational capacity results in heightened computing energy consumption. The results indicate that TTMCO adapts to changes in the computational capacity of MWDs and the scale of satellites deployment, enabling superior energy savings through the adjustment of computation offloading and resource allocation strategies.

paragraph_content.content: Fig. 9 shows LEO satellite’s altitude and system energy consumption at different maximum tolerable latency. When comparing LEO satellite orbital altitudes, there is a notable increase in system energy consumption as the altitude rises. This trend stems from the positive correlation between orbital altitude and transmission distance to MWDs. The elongated transmission distance results in higher transmission latency for task offloading, necessitating greater computational capacity allocation by satellites to meet latency requirements. Consequently, this leads to a significant rise in computing energy consumption. Moreover, the maximum tolerable latency of tasks has a positive impact on reducing the system energy consumption. With a higher maximum tolerable latency, MWDs can offload more tasks to LEO satellites and OBS for processing, thereby mitigating computing energy consumption. On the other hand, LEO satellites can meet the task processing latency requirements by allocating fewer computing resource.

paragraph_content.content: This paper designs a maritime edge computing system which aims to provide communication and computing services for MWDs. We formulate a non-convex energy consumption minimization problem. Specifically, to solve the MINLP problem, we decompose original problem into four subproblems and design algorithms to solve the corresponding subproblems. First, for the associated variable subproblem, we use slack variable method to transform the subproblem into a convex problem for solving. We solve joint transmission power optimization of MWDs and LEO satellites subproblem using quadratic transformation method. Then, the upper and lower bounds of offloading task size are obtained by deducing constraints, which are utilized for solving task partitioning subproblem. We solve joint computing resource optimization of LEO satellites and OBS subproblem using Lagrangian dual method and coordinate transformation method to obtain computing resource allocation. Thereafter, we design an iterative algorithm to jointly optimize the association variable, transmission power, task partitioning and computing resource allocation to obtain optimal variables to minimize system energy consumption. Finally, the performance of the proposed scheme in multiple environments is verified by simulation results. In the future, we will explore the complexity of the proposed scheme, challenges, and the key factors (e.g., spectrum resources) for scaling and deploying the scheme in real-world scenarios. In addition, we will study satellite-marine computing schemes in dynamic scenarios and consider designing UAV-assisted maritime edge computing systems.
